summary: This unit teaches the everyday calculations of a fabrication shop: units and conversions, fractions and inch sizes, percentages, ratio and proportion, lengths and angles, areas, volumes and masses, cut lists and sheet nesting, times, wages and job costs, tolerances and averages. You will learn a method that works for every calculation, how to round the right way for the job, and how to check your own and other people's working before steel is cut or a price is given.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). A Level 3 welder plans and leads work, so he or she must work out cut lists, material orders, weights, times and costs, and check the figures that team members bring. A wrong figure wastes steel, overloads a sling, misses a delivery date or loses money on a job.

The maths is not difficult, but it must be **right every time**. This kit gives you a method for every calculation, worked examples from the workshop, and the checks that catch mistakes before they cost anything.
**Who it is for:** Level 3 welding trainees, and anyone in a fabrication shop who plans jobs, orders material or prices work.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Read the drawing or job, put every figure into the same unit, use the right formula, and check the answer by estimate.
Work with fractions and inch sizes
Add, subtract, multiply and divide fractions; change inches to millimetres and fractions to decimals for old drawings and imported parts.
Work out mark-ups, margins, discounts, tax lines, mixing ratios, shares, and how time changes with the number of workers.
Work out lengths, angles and layouts
Perimeters, circumferences, rolled lengths, hole spacings, polygon and mitre angles, and frame diagonals.
Work out areas, volumes and masses
Plate and paint areas, tank capacities, and the mass of plate and sections for ordering and lifting.
Turn a drawing into a cut list, nest pieces into stock lengths and blanks into sheets, and work out bars to order and waste.
Work out times, wages and costs
Finish times, decimal hours, labour with overtime, energy and job costs.
Accept or reject measured parts, and use the mean, median, mode and range to understand results.
Round to the nearest, up or down as the job needs, and set out working so that someone else can check it.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with workshop calculations: fractions, percentages, proportion, cut lists, areas, volumes, masses, times, costs, averages, rounding and checking.
A **written paper**: short answers (a figure or a term), and longer answers where you must show every step and explain your checks.
**Practical tasks**: planning a cut list and material order for a batch of grilles and proving it by cutting a bar; and timing a small batch of parts, then costing it and forecasting a larger order.

blocks.note: Bring a calculator you know well. In the written paper, marks are given for the working, not only the answer: write the formula, the numbers, the units and your check.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Read the drawing or question; write down what you know, with units
Change every figure to the same unit
Write the formula in words or letters
Put in the numbers and work it out, keeping full figures in the calculator
Round only the final answer, in the way the job needs
Check it: rough estimate, does it make sense, are the units right?
Write the answer with its unit

head: Quantity
Units used
Conversions
rows: 1 kN = 1000 N; a 1 kg mass weighs about 9.81 N

blocks.note: Areas and volumes do not convert by 1000. A square metre is 1000 mm by 1000 mm, so it holds **one million** square millimetres. To change mm² to m², divide by 1 000 000; to change mm³ to m³, divide by 1 000 000 000.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Calculators and examiners follow **BODMAS**: Brackets first, then Orders (powers and roots), then Division and Multiplication, then Addition and Subtraction. So 6 + 4 × 3 = 18, but (6 + 4) × 3 = 30. When a formula has a line with a sum on top or below, put brackets round the top and the bottom before you divide: (1500 − 2 × 60) ÷ (6 − 1).

Before you trust a calculator answer, estimate. Round each number to one or two figures and work it out in your head. For 47 lengths at J$1 980 each: 50 × J$2 000 = about J$100 000. The exact answer, J$93 060, is close, so it is probably right. If the calculator had said J$9 306, you would know a digit was lost.

head: Round
When
Example
rows: Sizes and measurements: cut lengths, readings, reported results
732.3 mm to the nearest 0.5 mm is 732.5 mm; 732.2 mm is 732.0 mm
When you must have enough: bars, sheets, packets, tins, workers, days
When only complete items count: pieces from a bar, jobs that fit in the time or budget
12.9 pieces from a bar means 12 complete pieces

ul: **Decimal places** count digits after the point: 12.3456 to 2 decimal places is 12.35.
**Significant figures** count from the first digit that is not zero: 0.004 68 to 2 significant figures is 0.0047; 3 456 to 2 significant figures is 3 500.
To round to the nearest 0.5, look at which half-millimetre mark the figure is closest to.
Keep the full figure in the calculator and round only the final answer. Rounding part-way through lets small errors build into large ones.

blocks.h: Checking your own and other people's work

ul: **Estimate**: is the answer about the size you expected?
**Sense**: a plate two people can lift cannot weigh 45 tonnes; a tank on a house roof does not hold 50 000 litres.
**Units**: were metres and millimetres mixed? Was a radius used where the formula needs a diameter?
**Reverse**: work backwards from the answer (for example, divide the price by 1.2 to see if you get the cost back).
**Second person**: on a calculation sheet, someone else checks and initials each line.

blocks.note: When you find a mistake in a team member's working, go through it with them: show them how to put all sizes in one unit, write the formula first and check with an estimate. That stops the next mistake as well as this one.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Old drawings, imported parts, pipe and some plate and bar are still given in inches and fractions of an inch. You must be able to work with them and change them to millimetres.

ul: A fraction has a **numerator** (top) and a **denominator** (bottom). 3/4 means 3 parts out of 4.
**Simplest form:** divide top and bottom by the same number: 12/16 = 3/4.
**Mixed numbers** (such as 2 3/8) are changed to top-heavy fractions before you calculate: 2 3/8 = 19/8.

head: Operation
Method
Worked example
rows: Make the denominators the same, then add the tops
Make the denominators the same, then subtract the tops
Multiply the tops, multiply the bottoms, then simplify
Turn the second fraction upside down and multiply

ul: Fraction to decimal: divide the top by the bottom. 5/16 = 5 ÷ 16 = 0.3125.
Decimal inch to fraction: multiply by 16 (or 64) and put the result over 16 (or 64). 0.875 × 8 = 7, so 0.875 = 7/8.
Inches to millimetres: multiply by **25.4** (exact). Millimetres to inches: divide by 25.4.
Feet and inches: change to inches first. 6 ft 8 in = 80 in = 80 × 25.4 = 2032 mm.
Electrode sizes still often carry inch names: 3/32 inch is about 2.4 mm (sold as 2.4 or 2.5 mm), 1/8 inch is about 3.2 mm, 5/32 inch is about 4.0 mm.
Pipe is named by a **nominal size**, not its real diameter: a "2-inch" steel pipe has an outside diameter of about 60.3 mm. Use the pipe table, not × 25.4, for pipe.

Metric plate comes in sizes such as 3, 5, 6, 8, 10 and 12 mm, which do not match inch sizes exactly. If a drawing in inches must be made in metric plate, propose the nearest sizes to the supervisor and customer and get approval before ordering: a change in thickness can change the fit and the strength.

blocks.note: Convert once, write both values on the drawing or cut list, and have someone check them. Never let each person convert on the shop floor.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Task
Method
Worked example
rows: Find a percentage of an amount
Find the original before an increase (reverse)
A price of J$54 000 includes a 20% mark-up: cost = 54 000 ÷ 1.2 = J$45 000 (not 54 000 × 0.8)
Wire rose from J$4 200 to J$4 620 a box: 420 ÷ 4 200 × 100 = 10%
One amount as a percentage of another

ul: Decimals and percentages: multiply by 100 to get a percentage (0.065 = 6.5%); divide by 100 to get a decimal (12.5% = 0.125).
A percentage taken off and then added back does not return to the start, because the second percentage is of a different amount: J$50 000 less 10% is J$45 000; add 10% and you get J$49 500.

blocks.p: Both describe profit, but they divide it by different amounts. **Mark-up** is profit as a percentage of the **cost**. **Margin** is profit as a percentage of the **selling price**.

ul: A job costs J$60 000. With a 20% mark-up the price is 60 000 × 1.2 = J$72 000, and the profit is J$12 000.
The margin on that job is 12 000 ÷ 72 000 × 100 = 16.7%, not 20%.
For a 20% **margin**, the cost must be 80% of the price: price = 60 000 ÷ 0.8 = J$75 000.

head: Mark-up on cost
Same job as a margin on price

blocks.note: Say clearly which one you are using when you price a job, and check by working backwards. Confusing them means pricing too low.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: General consumption tax (GCT) is added to the price before tax **at the current rate**, which you must check, because rates change. Show it on its own line: GCT = price before tax × rate ÷ 100, and total = price before tax + GCT. Never take GCT off a total by subtracting the rate as a percentage of the total: that is the same reverse-percentage trap as above.

ul: A ratio compares amounts: 3 : 2. Simplify it like a fraction: 12 : 8 = 3 : 2.
**Sharing in a ratio:** add the parts, find one part, then multiply. J$90 000 shared 2 : 3 is 5 parts of J$18 000, so J$36 000 and J$54 000.
**Mixing ratios:** a two-pack paint mixed 4 : 1 by volume gives 5 L from 4 L of base and 1 L of hardener. For 3 L of base you need 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75 L of hardener.
**Scale:** on a 1 : 20 drawing, 1 mm on paper is 20 mm on the job. Use scale only to understand a drawing; work from the written sizes.

head: Kind
What it means
Worked example
rows: Both go up together at the same rate. Find the value for one, then multiply (the unitary method)
5 m of angle costs J$9 250, so 1 m costs J$1 850 and 17 m costs J$31 450
One goes up as the other comes down. Work out the total amount of work first
3 welders take 8 days: 3 × 8 = 24 worker-days. 4 welders need 24 ÷ 4 = 6 days

blocks.note: An inverse-proportion answer assumes the work can really be shared. Before you rely on it, check that there are enough welding sets, space, materials and supervision for the extra people, and that some jobs do not have to wait for others (such as paint drying). Always round people up: 4.2 workers means 5.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 × (length + width).
Circumference of a circle = **π × diameter**. Use π = 3.142 or the π key, as the question says.
Diameter from circumference = circumference ÷ π.
Length of an arc = angle ÷ 360 × π × diameter. A 90° corner of 150 mm radius: 90 ÷ 360 × 3.142 × 300 = 235.65 mm.

blocks.p: When flat bar or plate is rolled into a ring, the inside stretches less than the outside. Work out the blank length on the **mean diameter**, the diameter through the middle of the thickness: mean diameter = inside diameter + thickness (or outside diameter − thickness).
Example: 12 mm flat bar rolled to an inside diameter of 800 mm. Mean diameter = 800 + 12 = 812 mm. Length = 3.142 × 812 = **2551.3 mm**. Using the inside diameter would give a ring that is too small.

A slot with fully rounded ends is two straight sides plus one full circle. Straight length = overall length − width. Example: a slot 60 mm long overall and 16 mm wide: straights 2 × (60 − 16) = 88 mm, plus 3.142 × 16 = 50.3 mm, so the cut is about **138.3 mm** long.

head: Rule
Use
rows: A right angle is 90°; a straight line 180°; a full turn 360°
Checking squareness and angles on drawings
The angles of a triangle add up to 180°
Gussets and braces: two angles of 90° and 40° leave 50°
The angles of any four-sided shape add up to 360°
Frames and plates with angled corners
Each inside angle of a regular shape with n sides = (n − 2) × 180 ÷ n
Holes spaced equally round a pitch circle: angle = 360 ÷ number of holes
Frame mitres: for a regular frame with n sides, cut each end 180 ÷ n degrees off square

ul: Holes along a bar with a hole at each end: number of spaces = number of holes − 1. Spacing = distance between the end holes ÷ number of spaces.
Bars inside a frame with equal clear gaps: number of gaps = number of bars + 1. **Clear gap = (inside width − number of bars × bar width) ÷ (number of bars + 1).**
Example: 9 bars of 16 mm in an inside width of 1500 mm: (1500 − 144) ÷ 10 = **135.6 mm** clear gap; the centres are 135.6 + 16 = 151.6 mm apart.
Mark out from one datum (one end or edge) rather than from mark to mark, so that small errors do not add up.

blocks.p: For a right-angled triangle, the longest side (c) is found from **c² = a² + b²** (Pythagoras). So the diagonal of a rectangular frame = √(length² + width²).

ul: Example: a frame 1200 mm × 500 mm: √(1 440 000 + 250 000) = √1 690 000 = **1300 mm**. Both diagonals should read 1300 mm; if they differ, the frame is out of square.
The **3-4-5 rule** sets out a right angle with a tape: 600, 800 and 1000 mm make a perfect right-angled triangle.
The side of a square plate from its area: side = √area. A square plate of 0.36 m² has sides of √0.36 = 0.6 m = 600 mm.

head: Shape
Area
rows: Trapezium (two parallel sides a and b)

blocks.p: For a shape made of several parts, add the parts or take away the pieces cut out. Example: a 400 × 300 mm base plate with two corners cut off as triangles with 50 mm legs, and one hole of 40 mm diameter: 120 000 − 2 × (½ × 50 × 50) − 3.142 × 20² = 120 000 − 2 500 − 1 256.8 = **116 243.2 mm²**, or about 0.116 m².

blocks.note: In a circle formula, use the **radius** (half the diameter) with π × r². Squaring the diameter by mistake makes the area four times too big.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: A shape with the same section all along (a prism, plate, bar or tank): volume = area of the end × length.
Rectangular tank: length × width × depth. 1.5 m × 1.2 m × 1.0 m = 1.8 m³ = **1800 L**.
Cylinder (round tank, round bar, pipe bore): π × radius² × length. A tank 1.4 m across and 1.6 m deep: 3.142 × 0.7² × 1.6 = 2.463 m³, about **2 463 L**.
1 m³ = 1000 L. One litre of water has a mass of about 1 kg, so a full 2 463 L tank holds about 2.5 tonnes of water, plus the tank itself: the stand must carry it.

blocks.p: **Mass = volume × density.** Work the volume out in m³ and multiply by the density in kg/m³.

ul: **Quick rule for steel plate:** 1 m² of steel weighs 7.85 kg for every millimetre of thickness. A 2.4 m × 1.2 m sheet of 10 mm plate: 2.88 m² × 78.5 kg = **226 kg**.
Round bar: π × r² × length × 7850. A 20 mm bar weighs 3.142 × 0.01² × 7850 = about 2.47 kg per metre.
**Section tables** give the mass per metre of angle, channel, beams and tube. Mass = kg per metre × total length. Example: 18 pieces of 1.4 m of a tube listed at 4.25 kg/m: 25.2 m × 4.25 = 107.1 kg.
For a plate with holes, work out the area of the holes and take it away before you multiply by thickness and density.

blocks.note: Work out the mass of every heavy item before it is lifted, and check that the sling, shackle and hoist are rated for it. Never guess a weight.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: A flat plate has two faces and four edges: area = 2 × length × width, plus the edges if they are thick.
Section tables often give the **surface area per metre** (m²/m) of angles, channels and tubes. Multiply by the total length.
Paint needed (litres) = area × number of coats ÷ spreading rate (m² per litre). Round **up** to whole tins.

sections.title: Cut lists, stock lengths and sheet nesting

blocks.p: A cut list turns a drawing into the pieces the saw must cut. Put every size in millimetres and list each different piece once, with its quantity per item and the total for the batch.

These are pieces for a 1200 × 800 mm frame with butt joints: the top and bottom run the full width, and each side is 800 − 2 × 40 = 720 mm, because it fits between them. With mitred corners every piece would be cut to the full outside size, measured on the long point.

ul: Each saw cut turns a strip of steel into swarf: the **kerf**. Allow it for every piece you cut.
**Pieces per bar** = bar length ÷ (piece length + kerf), rounded **down**.
**Offcut** = bar length − pieces × (piece length + kerf).
**Bars to order** = pieces needed ÷ pieces per bar, rounded **up**.
If the bar ends are damaged or not square, allow a trim cut at the start.

blocks.p: Example, with 6 m bars and a 3 mm kerf: 6000 ÷ 1203 = 4.99, so only **4** pieces of 1200 mm come from one bar (five would need 6015 mm). The offcut is 6000 − 4 × 1203 = 1188 mm.

blocks.h: Planning the cutting: mix the pieces

blocks.p: Cutting each size from its own bars often wastes steel. Plan the longest pieces first, then fill the gaps with shorter ones. For the 5 frames above:

head: Plan
Bars needed
Offcuts
rows: Each size from its own bars: 4 × 1200 per bar, 8 × 720 per bar
3 bars for the 1200s (4 + 4 + 2) and 2 for the 720s (8 + 2): 5 bars
Mixed: 3 × 1200 and 3 × 720 per bar (5778 mm with kerfs)
3 bars give 9 of each; a fourth bar gives the last 1200 and 720: 4 bars
222 mm on each of the first three bars; 4074 mm on the last

ul: The least possible: total length with kerfs = 10 × 1203 + 10 × 723 = 19 260 mm, which is 3.2 bars, so at least **4** bars are needed. The mixed plan reaches it.
**Waste %** = (steel bought − steel in the pieces) ÷ steel bought × 100. Here (24 000 − 19 200) ÷ 24 000 × 100 = 20%.
The 4074 mm offcut is useful stock: label it with its section (and heat number on traceable work) and rack it. Counting it as stock, the true waste is only 726 mm, about 3%.
Write the plan one line per bar so the person cutting can follow it and tick off each piece.
Blanks along each side = sheet side ÷ blank side, rounded **down**. Total = blanks along the length × blanks along the width.
Always try both ways round, and see whether the strip left over can take more blanks turned the other way.
Allow for the cut width (kerf) for plasma, gas or saw cutting when the blanks are tight.

blocks.p: Example: blanks 450 × 280 mm from a 2440 × 1220 mm sheet. One way: 2440 ÷ 450 = 5 and 1220 ÷ 280 = 4, so **20** blanks. The other way: 2440 ÷ 280 = 8 and 1220 ÷ 450 = 2, so only 16. Use the first layout.

blocks.note: Sheet and plate are often sold in Jamaica in sizes such as 8 ft × 4 ft (about 2440 × 1220 mm). Check the real size of the sheet you have before you nest, not the size you expect.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: There are 60 minutes in an hour, so time is not decimal. Decimal hours to minutes: multiply the decimal part by 60. 3.7 h = 3 h + 0.7 × 60 min = **3 h 42 min** (not 3 h 70 min).
Hours and minutes to decimal hours: divide the minutes by 60. 2 h 45 min = 2 + 45 ÷ 60 = 2.75 h.
Minutes to hours: divide by 60. 2 640 min = 44 h.
Add hours, then minutes; if the minutes reach 60 or more, carry an hour. 06:50 + 4 h 35 min = 10:85 = **11:25**.
Time between two clock times: count to the next whole hour, then on. 08:40 to 14:15 = 20 min + 5 h + 15 min = 5 h 35 min = 335 min.
If a break falls inside the working period, add it on: work of 5 h from 09:00 with a 30-minute lunch at noon finishes at 14:30.
Working hours per day = time at work − breaks. 07:30 to 16:30 with a 1-hour lunch gives 8 working hours.
Labour cost = hours × hourly rate, worked out for each person and each kind of hours.
Overtime at **time and a half** is paid at 1.5 × the normal rate; double time at 2 ×.
Example: a welder at J$1 050 an hour works 40 normal hours and 6 hours at time and a half. 40 × 1 050 = J$42 000; overtime rate 1 050 × 1.5 = J$1 575; 6 × 1 575 = J$9 450; total **J$51 450**.
Set the working out as a table, one line per person and kind of hours, so it is easy to check. Add the hours too, as a check.

flow: Materials: quantity × unit price for each item (per length, per kg, per sheet)
Consumables: electrodes or wire, gas, discs, paint
Labour: hours × rates, with overtime shown separately
Overheads, if the shop adds them
Total cost, then the mark-up gives the price before tax
GCT at the current rate on its own line, then the total to pay

ul: Unit price = total price ÷ quantity: a 20 kg reel of wire at J$18 600 costs J$930 per kg.
Time for a batch = time per item × number of items, plus any set-up time once.
**Power (W) = volts × amps.** An arc at 22 V and 180 A uses 3 960 W, or 3.96 kW.
A machine takes more power from the supply than it delivers to the arc. Supply power = arc power ÷ efficiency: at 85%, 3.96 ÷ 0.85 = 4.66 kW. (Dividing makes it bigger, which must be right.)
**Energy (kWh) = power (kW) × time (h).** For 2.5 hours of arc time: 4.66 × 2.5 = 11.65 kWh.
Cost = kWh × the price per kWh. At a made-up rate of J$70 per kWh, about J$815. The real cost is a little higher, because the machine also uses power while idle.
Duty cycle: a machine rated 60% can weld 0.6 × 10 = 6 minutes in every 10 at that current.

blocks.p: Write the formula, list what each letter stands for and its unit, then put the numbers in. For drill speed, **N = 1000 × S ÷ (π × D)**, where N is rev/min, S is the cutting speed in m/min and D is the drill size in mm. For S = 24 and D = 8: N = 24 000 ÷ (3.142 × 8) = 955 rev/min. Set the nearest speed the drill has, below the answer rather than above.

ul: A size of 640 ± 0.5 mm has limits of 639.5 and 640.5 mm. A part **on** a limit passes; anything outside fails.
Unequal tolerances: 25 +0.2 / −0 allows 25.0 to 25.2 mm.
Percentage within tolerance = parts in tolerance ÷ parts measured × 100.

head: Measure
How to find it
Best used when
rows: Add all the values and divide by how many there are
Values are fairly even, or you need a total (mean × number of items)
Put the values in order and take the middle one (or halfway between the two middle ones)
One or two values are unusually high or low and would pull the mean
The value that comes up most often
You want the most common size or count, such as the electrode size used most
You want to know how spread out the results are

blocks.p: Example: daily output of frames for a week of 7 days: 18, 22, 20, 21, 34, 19, 20. Mean = 154 ÷ 7 = 22. In order: 18, 19, 20, 20, 21, 22, 34, so the median is 20 and the mode is 20. The range is 34 − 18 = 16. The 34 (a day with extra helpers) pulls the mean up, so the median, 20, is the fairer picture of a normal day.

When measured parts fail, ask two questions. Is the **average** off target? Then the setting (a saw stop, a jig) needs adjusting. Is the **spread** (range) wider than the tolerance band? Then something makes the parts vary: loose clamping, a worn blade, burrs, measuring from different ends, or different people marking out. Moving the stop will not cure a spread problem.

ul: Use a table with a heading, the units in the column headings and one line per item.
Show the working under the results, step by step, so a checker can follow it.
State your assumptions, such as "6 m bars, 3 mm kerf" or "8 working hours a day".
Sign or initial your work, and have the checker initial theirs.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can follow a method for every calculation: same units, formula first, round at the end, check.
I can convert between mm and m, mm² and m², mm³, m³ and litres, and kg and tonnes.
I can use brackets and the order of operations on a calculator.
I can estimate an answer to check it, and round to the nearest, up or down as the job needs.
I can add, subtract, multiply and divide fractions and mixed numbers.
I can change fractions to decimals and inches to millimetres.
I can work out percentages, increases, decreases, reverse percentages and percentage change.
I can explain the difference between mark-up and margin and work out each.
I can add GCT on its own line at the current rate.
I can share in a ratio, use mixing ratios, and work with direct and inverse proportion.
I can work out perimeters, circumferences, rolled lengths using the mean diameter, and slot lengths.
I can work out polygon, mitre and pitch-circle angles, and equal spacings.
I can use Pythagoras to work out a frame diagonal.
I can work out the areas of rectangles, triangles, trapeziums, circles and composite shapes.
I can work out volumes and capacities of tanks, and the mass of plate and sections.
I can make a cut list, plan cutting to use the fewest bars, and work out offcuts and waste.
I can nest blanks in a sheet both ways round.
I can change decimal hours to hours and minutes and work out finish times with breaks.
I can work out labour cost with overtime, and a full job cost.
I can work out power, energy and electricity cost.
I can accept or reject parts against a tolerance, and use the mean, median, mode and range.

terms: Composite shape
A shape made up of simpler shapes added together or cut away
Cut list
A list of every piece to be cut, with section, length and quantity
Decimal hours
Time written as a decimal, such as 2.75 h for 2 h 45 min
Denominator
The bottom number of a fraction
Density
Mass per unit volume; steel is about 7850 kg/m³
Direct proportion
Two amounts that rise and fall together at the same rate
Estimate
A rough answer, worked out with rounded figures, used to check
GCT
General consumption tax, added to a price at the current rate
Inverse proportion
One amount rises as the other falls, such as workers and days
Kerf
The width of material lost in a saw or thermal cut
Margin
Profit as a percentage of the selling price
Mark-up
Profit as a percentage of the cost
Mean
The total of the values divided by how many there are
Mean diameter
The diameter through the middle of a ring's thickness, used for rolled lengths
Median
The middle value when the values are in order
Mode
The value that occurs most often
Nesting
Laying out pieces in a bar or sheet to use as little material as possible
Numerator
The top number of a fraction
Offcut
The material left over after the pieces are cut
Pitch circle diameter (PCD)
The diameter of the circle on which the centres of a ring of holes lie
Range
The highest value minus the lowest value
Ratio
A comparison of amounts, written like 3 : 2
Significant figures
The digits of a number counted from the first one that is not zero
Tolerance
The amount by which a size may vary from the size given
Worker-days
The number of workers multiplied by the number of days: the amount of work in a job

c1.title: Window grilles for a church hall in Linstead
c1.text: Tamara is planning eight window grilles for a church hall in Linstead, St Catherine. Each frame is 1100 mm wide and 900 mm high, in 25 × 25 mm square tube with butt joints: the top and bottom rails are 1100 mm, and the two sides fit between them at 850 mm. Inside each frame, seven upright bars of 16 mm square bar are spaced with equal clear gaps. The tube comes in 6 m lengths, and each saw cut loses 3 mm.

c2.title: A tank stand in Santa Cruz
c2.text: A farmer in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth, orders a stand for a round water tank 1.6 m across inside and 1.8 m high. The top of the stand is a 1.8 m × 1.8 m plate, 5 mm thick. The four legs are 2.4 m lengths of 75 × 75 × 6 mm angle (6.85 kg/m in the section table), and the eight braces are each 1.9 m of 50 × 50 × 5 mm angle (3.77 kg/m). The steel area to paint is 11.2 m², with two coats of a paint that covers 8 m² per litre. Use π = 3.142 and 7850 kg/m³ for steel.

c3.title: Pricing driveway gates in Falmouth
c3.text: Delroy is pricing a pair of driveway gates for a house in Falmouth, Trelawny. Materials cost J$38 400 and consumables J$4 600. The welder works 14 normal hours at J$1 100 an hour and 3 hours of overtime at time and a half; the helper works 14 hours at J$700 an hour. The shop adds a 30% mark-up to the total cost, then GCT on its own line at the current rate.

c4.title: A batch of shelf brackets in Morant Bay
c4.text: A team of three at a shop in Morant Bay, St Thomas, must make 120 shelf brackets. The team has timed the work at 22 minutes per bracket. The working day runs from 07:00 to 15:30, with a 30-minute lunch break at noon.

c5.title: Checking spacer bars in Port Antonio
c5.text: At a shop in Port Antonio, Portland, a saw is set to cut spacer bars drawn as 640 ± 0.5 mm. The first ten bars measure, in mm: 640.2, 639.6, 640.5, 640.6, 639.4, 640.0, 640.3, 639.5, 640.1 and 639.8.

questions.q: If seven 850 mm sides are cut from one 6 m length, with one cut for each piece, how long is the offcut?
questions.why: Each piece uses 850 + 3 = 853 mm, so seven use 5 971 mm, leaving 6 000 − 5 971 = 29 mm. Forgetting the kerf gives 50 mm; the kerf is real steel lost to every cut.

questions.q: Tamara plans each length to give three 1100 mm rails and three 850 mm sides. How many 6 m lengths does she need for all eight grilles?
questions.why: Three of each use 3 × 1103 + 3 × 853 = 5 868 mm, so one length gives three of each. Five lengths give 15 + 15 and one more gives the 16th rail and side: 6. Cutting each size from its own lengths would need 7.

questions.q: What is the clear gap between the upright bars in each frame?
questions.why: Inside width = 1100 − 2 × 25 = 1050 mm. Seven bars take 7 × 16 = 112 mm, leaving 938 mm for 7 + 1 = 8 gaps: 938 ÷ 8 = 117.25 mm. Using 7 gaps, or the outside width, gives the wrong spacing.

questions.q: With the six-length plan, what is the waste as a percentage of the tube bought, counting all offcuts and kerfs as waste?
questions.why: Bought: 6 × 6 000 = 36 000 mm. In the pieces: 16 × 1 100 + 16 × 850 = 31 200 mm. Waste = 4 800 ÷ 36 000 × 100 = 13.3%. Waste is a share of what was bought, so divide by 36 000, not by 31 200.

questions.q: About how many litres does the tank hold when full?
questions.why: Volume = π × r² × h = 3.142 × 0.8² × 1.8 = 3.62 m³, and 1 m³ = 1 000 L. Using the diameter as the radius gives four times too much; π × d × h gives a side area, not a volume.

questions.q: What is the mass of the top plate, to the nearest kilogram?
questions.why: Volume = 1.8 × 1.8 × 0.005 = 0.0162 m³; × 7 850 = 127 kg. Check with the quick rule: 3.24 m² × 7.85 kg × 5 mm = 127 kg. Keeping 5 mm as 0.05 m gives ten times too much.

questions.q: Using the section table, what is the total mass of the legs and braces?
questions.why: Legs: 4 × 2.4 = 9.6 m × 6.85 = 65.8 kg. Braces: 8 × 1.9 = 15.2 m × 3.77 = 57.3 kg. Total about 123 kg. Multiply each section's total length by its own kg per metre, then add.

questions.q: The paint is sold in 1-litre tins. How many tins should be bought for both coats?
questions.why: Paint = 11.2 m² × 2 coats ÷ 8 m² per litre = 2.8 L, rounded up to 3 tins, because part tins are bought whole. Forgetting the second coat gives 1.4 L; forgetting the spreading rate gives 22.4.

questions.q: What is the total labour cost for the gates?
questions.why: Welder 14 × 1 100 = 15 400; overtime 3 × 1 650 = 4 950 (1 100 × 1.5 = 1 650); helper 14 × 700 = 9 800. Total J$30 150. Paying overtime at the normal rate gives J$28 500.

questions.q: What is Delroy's price before GCT?
questions.why: Total cost = 38 400 + 4 600 + 30 150 = 73 150. With a 30% mark-up: 73 150 × 1.3 = J$95 095. Dividing by 0.7 gives a 30% margin, not a 30% mark-up; J$21 945 is the profit alone.

questions.q: The customer asks Delroy what share of his selling price is profit. What should he tell her?
questions.why: Profit J$21 945 ÷ price J$95 095 × 100 = 23.1%. A margin is profit over the selling price, so it is always smaller than the mark-up on the same job.

questions.q: The customer asks for 10% off the price before GCT. What profit would the job then make?
questions.why: New price = 95 095 × 0.9 = 85 585.50; profit = 85 585.50 − 73 150 = J$12 435.50. The discount comes off the price, so the costs stay the same and the whole J$9 509.50 comes off the profit.

questions.q: How much work is needed for the whole batch?
questions.why: 120 × 22 = 2 640 minutes, and 2 640 ÷ 60 = 44 hours. Reading 2 640 minutes as 26 h 40 min, or dividing by 100, treats time as if it were decimal.

questions.q: All three start at 07:00 on Monday and share the work equally. When will they finish?
questions.why: Each works 8 hours on Monday: 24 of the 44 hours. The other 20 hours are 6 h 40 min each on Tuesday. From 07:00 that is 13:40, plus the 30-minute lunch: 14:10. Reading 6.67 h as 6 h 67 min gives 14:37.

questions.q: The customer wants the batch finished in one working day. How many workers would that need?
questions.why: 44 hours ÷ 8 hours a day = 5.5 workers, rounded up to 6, because you cannot have half a worker and 5 would not finish. Check there are enough benches, tools and supervision before promising it.

questions.q: Before quoting 22 minutes, the team timed seven brackets: 20, 23, 21, 35, 22, 21 and 26 minutes. The 35 was when a drill bit broke. Which figure best shows the usual time?
questions.why: In order: 20, 21, 21, 22, 23, 26, 35, so the median is 22. The one-off 35 pulls the mean up to 24. The range shows spread, not a typical time.

questions.q: How many of the ten bars must be rejected?
questions.why: The limits are 639.5 and 640.5 mm. Only 640.6 and 639.4 are outside. Bars measuring exactly 639.5 and 640.5 are on the limits, so they pass.

questions.q: The ten readings average exactly 640.0 mm, yet two bars failed. What does this tell the team?
o: The batch passes, since the average is exactly on the drawn size
The stop must be moved 0.6 mm to bring the long bars in
The stop is right on average; something makes the lengths vary
The two bad bars were measured wrongly and can be passed
questions.why: A mean on target shows the setting is right. The range, 640.6 − 639.4 = 1.2 mm, is wider than the 1.0 mm tolerance band, so look for what causes the spread, such as clamping, the blade or burrs. Moving the stop would push other bars out.

questions.q: Sheldon builds a rectangular frame 1800 mm long and 1100 mm wide. What should each diagonal measure when it is square?
questions.why: Diagonal = √(1800² + 1100²) = √(3 240 000 + 1 210 000) = √4 450 000 = 2109.5 mm. Adding the sides, subtracting the squares, or averaging the sides does not give the diagonal.

questions.q: An old pump drawing gives a hole spacing of 4 3/8 inches. What is this in millimetres, to one decimal place?
questions.why: 4 3/8 = 4.375 inches, and 4.375 × 25.4 = 111.125, so 111.1 mm. Reading 3/8 as 0.3, ignoring the fraction, or rounding 4.375 to 4.38 before multiplying all give wrong answers.
